title: Jerusalem and Al-Aqsa
subtitle: Why Al-Aqsa matters in Islam and how to discuss Jerusalem with justice
summary: Al-Aqsa is the Farthest Mosque named in Quran 17:1 and identified with Jerusalem in authentic hadith. The Prophet named it among three mosques with a special status for travel in worship, and Muslims in Medina faced Jerusalem for sixteen or seventeen months before the qiblah changed to the Kaaba. Understanding the scripture, the sanctuary's names, and its shared setting helps Muslims honor it with accuracy and justice.

sections.title: Why Jerusalem and Al-Aqsa Matter in Islam
sections.body: For Muslims, Al-Aqsa is a place of revelation, prayer, and prophetic memory. Quran 17:1 names the Farthest Mosque and blesses its surroundings. Authentic hadith connects that mosque with Jerusalem, gives it a special place among mosques, and records Jerusalem as the first direction faced by the Muslim community in prayer.

sections.title: What the Name Al-Aqsa Refers To
sections.body:
The Arabic name al-Masjid al-Aqsa means "the Farthest Mosque." In common Muslim and custodial usage, Al-Aqsa Mosque or al-Haram al-Sharif refers to the whole walled sanctuary in Jerusalem. The Qibli prayer hall stands at its southern end, and the Dome of the Rock is a distinct building within the same sanctuary. A [Jordanian custodial description submitted through UNESCO](https://whc.unesco.org/document/181413) explains this wider use of the name.

Knowing the terms prevents a common mistake: the gold-domed building is the Dome of the Rock, not the Qibli prayer hall. Both stand within the wider Al-Aqsa sanctuary. Terminology can be politically contested, so careful writers should state which building or area they mean.

sections.title: The Isra and Mi'raj in Islamic Sources
sections.body:
Quran 17:1 states that Allah took His servant by night from al-Masjid al-Haram in Mecca to al-Masjid al-Aqsa, whose surroundings He blessed. The verse itself does not use the city-name Jerusalem. The location is made explicit in the Prophetic tradition: [Sahih al-Bukhari 3886](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3886) says Jerusalem was shown to the Prophet when he described his night journey, and [Sahih al-Bukhari 3888](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:3888) names Bayt al-Maqdis in its report of that journey.

The Prophet said that a special journey for worship is undertaken to three mosques: al-Masjid al-Haram, his mosque in Medina, and Al-Aqsa ([Sahih al-Bukhari 1189](https://sunnah.com/bukhari:1189)). [Sahih Muslim 525b](https://sunnah.com/muslim:525b) also records that Muslims faced Jerusalem for sixteen or seventeen months before the prayer direction changed to the Kaaba. These are strong and precise foundations for Al-Aqsa's importance in Islam.

sections.title: Sanctity Does Not Cancel Justice
sections.body:
Jerusalem is also sacred to Jews and Christians. Acknowledging that fact does not weaken Al-Aqsa's Islamic significance. It requires Muslims to speak accurately, protect human dignity, and reject religious hatred.

Quran 22:40 mentions monasteries, churches, synagogues, and mosques in a passage about people expelled from their homes and the protection of worship. It is an Islamic ethical foundation, not a modern property map or a substitute for historical and legal evidence. Questions about archaeology, access, administration, or sovereignty require their own reliable sources.

sections.title: Use the Right Evidence
sections.body: Use the Quran and authentic hadith to establish religious belief. Use inscriptions, archaeology, Islamic endowment (waqf) records, and dated documents for architectural and political history. Use current legal texts and reliable reporting for present disputes. Keeping these kinds of evidence separate makes the Islamic case clearer, not weaker.

sections.title: Key Takeaways: Jerusalem and Al-Aqsa
sections.body: Al-Aqsa's Islamic status rests on clear Quranic and Prophetic evidence. The name commonly includes the whole walled sanctuary, while the Qibli prayer hall and Dome of the Rock are distinct buildings within it. Muslims can defend Al-Aqsa's sacred character while using careful evidence and honoring the dignity of every innocent person.

quranVerses.arabic: بِسْمِ ٱللَّهِ ٱلرَّحْمَٰنِ ٱلرَّحِيمِ سُبْحَٰنَ ٱلَّذِىٓ أَسْرَىٰ بِعَبْدِهِۦ لَيْلًۭا مِّنَ ٱلْمَسْجِدِ ٱلْحَرَامِ إِلَى ٱلْمَسْجِدِ ٱلْأَقْصَا ٱلَّذِى بَٰرَكْنَا حَوْلَهُۥ لِنُرِيَهُۥ مِنْ ءَايَٰتِنَآ ۚ إِنَّهُۥ هُوَ ٱلسَّمِيعُ ٱلْبَصِيرُ
quranVerses.translation: Exalted is He who took His Servant by night from al-Masjid al-Haram to al-Masjid al-Aqsa, whose surroundings We have blessed, to show him of Our signs. Indeed, He is the Hearing, the Seeing.
quranVerses.sourceAttribution: api.alquran.cloud — Tanzil Uthmani text; Saheeh International translation

quranVerses.arabic: ٱلَّذِينَ أُخْرِجُوا۟ مِن دِيَٰرِهِم بِغَيْرِ حَقٍّ إِلَّآ أَن يَقُولُوا۟ رَبُّنَا ٱللَّهُ ۗ وَلَوْلَا دَفْعُ ٱللَّهِ ٱلنَّاسَ بَعْضَهُم بِبَعْضٍۢ لَّهُدِّمَتْ صَوَٰمِعُ وَبِيَعٌۭ وَصَلَوَٰتٌۭ وَمَسَٰجِدُ يُذْكَرُ فِيهَا ٱسْمُ ٱللَّهِ كَثِيرًۭا ۗ وَلَيَنصُرَنَّ ٱللَّهُ مَن يَنصُرُهُۥٓ ۗ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَقَوِىٌّ عَزِيزٌ
quranVerses.translation: [They are] those who have been evicted from their homes without right - only because they say, "Our Lord is Allah." And were it not that Allah checks the people, some by means of others, there would have been demolished monasteries, churches, synagogues, and mosques in which the name of Allah is much mentioned. And Allah will surely support those who support Him. Indeed, Allah is Powerful and Exalted in Might.

furtherReading.title: Jerusalem: The Contested City

furtherReading.note: A scholarly political history of modern Jerusalem that helps readers understand the city's modern divisions and competing claims.

furtherReading.title: Jerusalem: A Biography
furtherReading.author: Simon Sebag Montefiore
furtherReading.note: A broad narrative history useful for orientation; it should be read alongside specialist scholarship and primary sources.

furtherReading.title: Medieval Jerusalem and Islamic Worship: Holy Places, Ceremonies, Pilgrimage
furtherReading.author: Amikam Elad
furtherReading.note: A specialist history of Muslim worship and holy places in early and medieval Jerusalem, based on Arabic sources.
